messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 61

He is 68, a psychologist who has spent most of his adult life listening carefully to other people’s pain, and it still unsettles him that his own story begins in a way he did not recognize for what it was. When he talks about his former partner, he does not begin with fear. He begins with charm, intelligence, the kind of intensity that once felt flattering. They meet in his late fifties, after a period of loneliness he rarely admits to. He is established in his work, respected by colleagues, married now but speaking about an earlier relationship that lasted several years and left a deeper mark than he understood at the time. He says that at first the cruelty arrives in fragments—sarcasm disguised as honesty, anger explained away as stress, accusations that leave him apologizing for things he has not done.

The first time she hits him, they are in the kitchen. He remembers the hard brightness of the overhead light, the smell of coffee gone stale, and the shocking speed with which an argument about a missed phone call becomes physical. She slaps him across the face, then immediately tells him he has driven her to it by being cold and condescending. He stands there, stunned, one hand on the counter, noticing not pain so much as disbelief. He has worked with trauma survivors; he knows what abuse is supposed to look like. Yet in his own home, in his own life, he starts searching for nuance, context, some explanation that will preserve his sense of himself as perceptive and competent.

The violence becomes intermittent and therefore, in some ways, more binding. A shove into a doorway. Fingers digging into his arm hard enough to leave crescents. Once, during an argument in the car, she strikes him in the temple while he is driving. He pulls over and feels his heart pound so violently that he thinks, absurdly, of a panic attack in one of his patients and is ashamed of the comparison. After each incident, she cries or rages or insists he is exaggerating. He becomes careful in the ways abused people often do without naming it as such. He monitors her tone when he comes through the door. He rehearses harmless responses. He keeps his body angled, alert to distance and exits. He stops inviting friends over because he cannot bear the strain of pretending or the risk that they might see.

His work changes first in small ways. In session, he finds himself losing the thread when a patient raises their voice or describes domestic conflict. He is still thoughtful, still skilled, but internally he is braced. If someone closes the office door too sharply, his shoulders jump. He begins leaving more time between appointments so he can sit alone and steady his breathing. He tells himself he is tired, overworked, aging. At home, sleep becomes thin and unreliable. He wakes at 3 a.m. with his jaw clenched, hearing the crack of her hand against his face before he is fully awake. Sometimes he gets out of bed and checks the locks, though she no longer lives with him by then. In the morning, he feels foolish and unmoored.

The relationship ends after an assault in which she corners him in the hallway and repeatedly strikes his chest and neck while screaming that he is ruining her life. What he remembers most is not the pain but the sudden conviction that something catastrophic is about to happen, that he may fall, hit his head, or provoke even more violence if he tries to defend himself. He leaves the flat that night with his wallet, keys, and a briefcase full of patient notes. He sits in his car for nearly an hour, unable to drive, ashamed that what finally pushes him out is fear for his physical safety rather than some clearer moral line.

Now, years later, he is remarried to a kind woman who knows the outline of what happened, though he still struggles to speak about it without minimizing. He startles when she approaches him from behind in the kitchen. If a disagreement begins to sharpen, he feels his chest tighten and his mind go blank, as if language itself abandons him. He avoids certain streets near the old neighborhood. He has thrown away shirts with stiff collars because pressure at the neck makes him feel trapped. Intimacy is complicated; tenderness can suddenly tip into vigilance, and he hates the look of concern on his wife’s face when he pulls away for reasons he cannot explain quickly enough.

What distresses him most is the persistence of it. He knows, professionally and intellectually, that trauma imprints itself in fragments of sensation and expectation. But he is still humiliated by how easily he is transported. A patient mentions being mocked by a spouse, and he is back in that kitchen under the bright light, flooded with the same disbelief. He still catches himself listening for footsteps that are not there. He still scans moods in a room before he can attend to words. The life he has built in the aftermath is real—his marriage, his practice, his routines—but so is the private sense that danger can emerge without warning inside what ought to be safest.
